pula.intro: Pula's two remarkable trees both stand outside the city. On Veli Brijun, in Brijuni National Park, an olive split by a 1970s storm still gives oil every October; the park puts it at about 1,600 years from a 1960s carbon test, while others say only more than a thousand. It is a day trip by road to Fažana and the park's boat. In Medulin, south of Pula, a hackberry of about 115 years shades the main square and was Croatia's Tree of the Year in 2020.
pula.meta_description: Old trees near Pula: the Brijuni olive, about 1,600 years by the park's figure, and Medulin's hackberry, Croatia's Tree of the Year 2020.
pula.question_meta: The oldest tree near Pula is the olive on Veli Brijun, about 1,600 years by Brijuni National Park's figure, a dating others question.
pula.question_answer: The oldest tree near Pula is the old olive on Veli Brijun in Brijuni National Park, which the park puts at about 1,600 years from a carbon-14 test made in the 1960s. Other sources say only that Brijuni's oldest olives are more than a thousand years old, and a new dating was announced in 2017.
pula.question_context: Neither tree stands in Pula itself. The Brijuni olive is on Veli Brijun, the main island of Brijuni National Park, reached by road to Fažana, north-west of Pula, and then by the park's ticketed boat. The park says a trunk sample tested at the Ruđer Bošković Institute in Zagreb in the 1960s gave about 1,600 years. In 2017 the park, the Zagreb Faculty of Agriculture and the same institute announced a fresh dating of the islands' oldest olives, because the most anyone could say for certain was more than a thousand years; we have not found the results. The tree is about six metres tall, was split in two by a storm in the 1970s, and still yields about 30 kilograms of olives each October. The second tree is a Mediterranean hackberry on the main square of Medulin, at the southern tip of Istria, about 115 years old by local sources of 2020 and 2021. It won Croatia's Tree of the Year in 2020 and represented the country in the European contest in 2021. The two trees are a separate trip each.

faq.q: Can you visit the old olive on Brijuni?
faq.a: Yes, with a park ticket. Veli Brijun is reached only by the Brijuni National Park boat from Fažana, and the olive is on the visitor route. We have not confirmed current prices or crossing times.

faq.q: How old is the Brijuni olive?
faq.a: About 1,600 years by the park's figure, from a carbon-14 test made in the 1960s. Other sources say only more than a thousand years, and a new dating was announced in 2017.

faq.q: What is the tree on Medulin's main square?
faq.a: A Mediterranean hackberry of about 115 years, known as Najstarija Medulinka, the eldest resident of Medulin. It was Croatia's Tree of the Year in 2020.

rab.intro: Rab's remarkable tree is a holm oak with a birthday. It was planted on the Pjaceta, the Square of Freedom, on 23 April 1921, the day the Italian military left the island, and a century later its crown shades the whole square. Many Rab families tell of an ancestor who helped plant it. It was voted Croatian Tree of the Year in 2024 and finished ninth in the European Tree of the Year in 2025.
rab.meta_description: Rab's Tree of Freedom: a holm oak planted on 23 April 1921 on the Pjaceta, Croatian Tree of the Year 2024. Where it stands and its story.
rab.question_meta: Rab's best-known tree is the Tree of Freedom, a holm oak planted on the Pjaceta on 23 April 1921.
rab.question_answer: Rab's best-known tree is the Tree of Freedom, a holm oak planted on the Pjaceta in Rab's old town on 23 April 1921 to mark the departure of the Italian military. It was voted Croatian Tree of the Year in 2024.
rab.question_context: The Tree of Freedom is about 105 years old, and unlike most ages on this map, that number is a planting date rather than an estimate. The town planted it on 23 April 1921, the day the Italian military left Rab, on the small square that takes its name, the Pjaceta or Square of Freedom. Its centenary was celebrated in 2021, by which time the crown shaded the whole square. Many families on the island keep a tradition that an ancestor took part in the planting, a story repeated on its European Tree of the Year entry. The Society of Friends of Rab nominated it for Croatian Tree of the Year, which it won in 2024, and in 2025 it represented Croatia in the European contest, finishing ninth with 12,807 votes. Nobody has published its height or girth. The square is in the old town of Rab, on the island of the same name, which is reached by ferry from the mainland; once in town, the tree is a short walk from anywhere. It is free to see at any hour.

faq.q: When was Rab's Tree of Freedom planted?
faq.a: On 23 April 1921, to mark the departure of the Italian military from Rab. That makes it about 105 years old in 2026.

faq.q: Where is the Tree of Freedom on Rab?
faq.a: On the Pjaceta, the Square of Freedom, in Rab's old town. It is the big crown that shades the whole square, free to see at any hour.

lun.intro: Lun, at the northern tip of Pag, has some 24 hectares of olive groves protected as a botanical reserve since 1963, with dry-stone walls nearly two metres high between them. The oldest tree stands a metre or two from the old road at the entrance, where the marked path begins. Local experts put it at about 2,000 years from a trunk about four metres across; other local sources say more than 1,600. A newspaper caption nicknamed it Metuzalemka.
lun.meta_description: Lun's oldest olive on Pag, 1,600 to 2,000 years by local estimates, at the entrance to the olive gardens protected since 1963.
lun.question_meta: Lun's oldest olive is put at 1,600 to 2,000 years by local estimates and stands at the entrance to the Lun olive gardens.
lun.question_answer: The oldest olive at Lun, on Pag, is put at between 1,600 and 2,000 years by local estimates and stands beside the old road at the entrance to the olive gardens. The 2,000-year figure is arithmetic from a trunk about four metres across, not a measured date.
lun.question_context: The estimate of about 2,000 years comes from experts of the Lun olive cooperative and the Zagreb Faculty of Agronomy, quoted by the newspaper Novi list in 2021. They took a trunk about four metres across and a growth of about a millimetre of width a year. That is a rough method, and an old olive is often a hollow trunk of several stems, so other local sources stop at more than 1,600 years. The groves around the tree cover about 24 hectares on the northern tip of the island of Pag and were protected as a botanical reserve in 1963. Total Croatia News counts about 80,000 old olives there and around 1,500 ancient wild ones. Marked paths between high dry-stone walls let you walk the groves without a guide. An entrance fee in season has been reported, but we have not confirmed the price or hours. Our pin is approximate, at the entrance end of the groves where the oldest tree stands.

faq.q: How old are the Lun olives?
faq.a: The oldest is put at between 1,600 and 2,000 years by local estimates, and Total Croatia News says many in the groves are believed to be over 1,500. None of these figures is a measured date.

faq.q: Where is the oldest olive in Lun?
faq.a: A metre or two from the old road at the entrance to the Lun olive gardens, where the marked path into the groves begins.

kastela.intro: Kaštela, the string of seven towns between Split and Trogir, has two protected trees on the local bus line. In Kaštel Štafilić stands Mastrinka, an olive ten metres tall with a trunk six metres round, reported at more than 1,500 years and still harvested by the town each autumn. In Kaštel Gomilica a downy oak grows beside the Romanesque church of St Cosmas and Damian, built between 1138 and 1160, protected for its beauty and size.
kastela.meta_description: Kaštela's protected trees: Mastrinka, an olive reported at over 1,500 years in Kaštel Štafilić, and the downy oak by a 12th-century church.
kastela.question_meta: Kaštela's oldest tree is Mastrinka, an olive in Kaštel Štafilić reported at more than 1,500 years, protected since 1990.
kastela.question_answer: Kaštela's oldest tree is Mastrinka, the olive of Kaštel Štafilić, reported at more than 1,500 years and protected as a natural monument since 1990. No source we found explains how that age was worked out, so read it as a popular figure.
kastela.question_context: Mastrinka is ten metres tall with a crown 22 metres across and a trunk six metres round, and the Kaštela tourist board says its roots spread through more than 100 metres of ground. The 1,500-year figure is repeated everywhere, but nobody has published a method; one listing claims over 2,000. Total Croatia News says its variety is found nowhere else in Croatia or the region and was probably brought from southern Italy or Greece, the article's claim rather than a botanical finding. It is still harvested every autumn with the town taking part, and October 2025 brought a record crop. It is reported to stand in the courtyard of the Maslina kindergarten, and a visitor point with benches was announced in 2018; we have not confirmed when it can be seen. The second tree is a downy oak by the church of St Cosmas and Damian in Kaštel Gomilica, protected since 1996, with no published age or size. Both towns are stops on the Split to Trogir local bus.

faq.q: How old is the olive of Kaštel Štafilić?
faq.a: It is reported at more than 1,500 years, a figure no source we found explains. It has been a protected natural monument since 1990.

faq.q: Can you visit the Kaštel Štafilić olive?
faq.a: It is reported to stand in the courtyard of the Maslina kindergarten. A public visitor point was announced in 2018, but we have not confirmed it exists or when the tree can be seen.

faq.q: Where is the oak in Kaštel Gomilica?
faq.a: Beside the Romanesque church of St Cosmas and Damian, built between 1138 and 1160. It is a downy oak, protected as a natural monument since 1996.

zadar.intro: Zadar's remarkable tree is a drive away. The Green Oak of Islam Latinski, about 20 km north of the city beside the old Zagreb to Zadar road, keeps its thick green leaves until about the end of February. It is a hybrid oak of unknown origin whose parents botanists have debated for decades, and a 2018 DNA study sampled it. Croatia protected it in 1957; a 2009 blog puts it at about 250 years and calls it the old Wolf's Oak.
zadar.meta_description: The Green Oak of Islam Latinski, 20 km north of Zadar: a hybrid oak green until February, protected since 1957, its parentage still debated.
zadar.question_meta: Near Zadar, the Green Oak of Islam Latinski is a hybrid oak that stays green until about the end of February.
zadar.question_answer: The best-known old tree near Zadar is the Green Oak, Zeleni hrast, in Islam Latinski, about 20 km north of the city. It is a single hybrid oak that keeps its leaves green until about the end of February, protected since 1957.
zadar.question_context: The Green Oak is known to botanists as Quercus x viridis, a hybrid whose parents have been argued over. Earlier authors proposed Turkey oak crossed with holm oak, or Turkey oak crossed with cork oak. A 2018 study in the Croatian forestry journal Šumarski list ran DNA on this tree and others and did not support holm oak as a parent, which the authors read as favouring Turkey oak and cork oak, though they word that carefully. Croatia protected the tree in 1957. Its age is not measured. A 2009 blog reports about 250 years, says it was once called Wolf's Oak and thought magical, and describes it as a boundary marker with earlier oaks of the same kind on the same spot. The most recent evidence that it stands is the 2018 study, and our pin is the register's point beside the road, not a fix on the trunk. Islam Latinski is in Posedarje municipality, roughly 20 to 25 minutes from Zadar by car; we found no confirmed bus.

faq.q: Why is it called the Green Oak?
faq.a: Because it keeps thick green leaves until about the end of February, which is where the name Zeleni hrast comes from.

faq.q: How do you get to the Green Oak from Zadar?
faq.a: By car, about 20 km north on the old Zagreb to Zadar road to Islam Latinski, roughly 20 to 25 minutes. It is seen from beside the road.

brac.intro: Brač's protected tree is an oddity rather than an ancient. In the inland village of Nerežišća, a pine about 170 centimetres tall grows out of the roof of the church of St Peter and Paul, with no roots found reaching the ground. Officials estimate it at about 120 years, with uncertainty, and Croatia declared it a natural monument in 1969 as a rare specimen. It is seen from the street, so the church need not be open.
brac.meta_description: The pine on the church roof in Nerežišća, Brač: about 170 cm tall, around 120 years by an official guess, protected since 1969.
brac.question_meta: Brač's best-known tree is a pine growing from the roof of the church of St Peter and Paul in Nerežišća.
brac.question_answer: Brač's best-known tree is the pine on the roof of the church of St Peter and Paul in Nerežišća, about 170 centimetres tall and protected as a natural monument since 1969. Officials estimate it at about 120 years, and say they are not sure.
brac.question_context: The pine is the draw because of where it grows, not its size or age. Total Croatia News reported in 2017 that it stands 170 centimetres tall on the roof of the church of St Peter and Paul, that no roots have been found reaching the ground, and that it lives on rainwater. Officials put it at about 120 years with uncertainty. One island guide identifies it as a miniature black pine. The church itself is given as about 600 years old by Total Croatia News, and as 13th or 14th century by other sources. Croatia protected the tree in 1969 as a rare specimen. Nerežišća lies inland, reached from the ferry port at Supetar by island bus or car, and the roof is visible from the street in the village centre, so there are no opening hours to worry about. The most recent dated report of the pine that we found is from 2017, so a visitor who sees it now knows more than we do.

faq.q: Where is the tree on the church roof on Brač?
faq.a: On the church of St Peter and Paul in the centre of Nerežišća, an inland village reached from Supetar. It is seen from the street.

faq.q: How old is the Nerežišća roof pine?
faq.a: About 120 years by an official estimate that admits its uncertainty. It is about 170 centimetres tall.

hvar.intro: Hvar's oldest tree grows in the courtyard of the Franciscan monastery, a short walk east of the main square along the quay. It is a horizontal-branched cypress, 300 to 350 years old by a 2000 scientific estimate, seven metres tall, its trunk forking into an umbrella. Tradition says the Italian painter Matteo Rosselli planted it while convalescing at the monastery; the same study notes there is no written proof. It has been protected since 1961.
hvar.meta_description: Rosselli's cypress at Hvar's Franciscan monastery: 300 to 350 years by a 2000 study, an umbrella-shaped cypress with a painter's legend.
hvar.question_meta: Hvar's oldest known tree is the cypress in the Franciscan monastery courtyard, 300 to 350 years old by a 2000 study.
hvar.question_answer: Hvar's oldest known tree is the cypress in the courtyard of the Franciscan monastery, which a 2000 scientific study put at 300 to 350 years. Tour guides say 500 years, but no source supports that figure.
hvar.question_context: The tree is known as Roselijev čempres, Rosselli's cypress, after the tradition that the Italian painter Matteo Rosselli, who lived from 1578 to 1650, planted it while recovering from an illness at the monastery. A genetic study published in Šumarski list in 2000 records the tradition and says plainly that no written proof exists. The same study describes it as the horizontal-branched form of the Mediterranean cypress, seven metres tall with no upright leader, its trunk forking two ways into an umbrella with branches seven to eight metres long. Around 2000 its trunk measured 220 centimetres round at 1.5 metres, and its heart had rotted, leaving 10 to 15 centimetres of living wood. The genetics suggested an introduced tree. It was declared a protected natural rarity in 1961. Two younger cypresses in the same courtyard were planted in 1963. The monastery lies about five to eight minutes' walk east of the main square and charges for entry; we could not confirm current hours.

faq.q: Can you see the cypress at Hvar's Franciscan monastery?
faq.a: Yes, inside the monastery's garden and museum, which charge for entry. Third-party guides list roughly 3 to 10 euro; we could not confirm current opening hours.

faq.q: Did Matteo Rosselli plant the Hvar cypress?
faq.a: That is the tradition and the source of its local name, but the 2000 study of the tree says no written proof exists. The study dates it to 300 to 350 years.

cara.intro: Čara, a village on Korčula about 25 kilometres by road from Korčula town, is dominated, in the Croatian tourist board's words, by its parish church of St Peter and a century-old cypress the villagers are proud of. The cypress has been on Croatia's register of protected natural monuments since 1948. Its age is a puzzle: the tourist board says a century, other tourism pages say 500 years, and nobody has measured it.
cara.meta_description: The cypress of Čara on Korčula: a protected tree beside the parish church of St Peter, a century to 500 years old depending on the source.
cara.question_meta: Čara's old cypress stands by the parish church of St Peter on Korčula; its age is put anywhere from a century to 500 years.
cara.question_answer: The cypress of Čara stands beside the parish church of St Peter in the centre of the village, on Korčula, and has been a protected natural monument since 1948. The tourist board calls it century-old; other pages say 500 years, and none of these ages comes from a measurement.
cara.question_context: Very little has been written about the Čara cypress, and what has been written disagrees. Croatia's tourist board says the village is dominated by the parish church of St Peter and a century-old cypress that locals are particularly proud of. Other tourism pages put the tree at 500 years. The gap between the two figures is four centuries, and neither is based on a measured date, so it is best read as an old cypress of unknown age. It is one tree, entered on the national register of protected natural monuments in 1948. The church beside it dates from the 15th or 16th century, depending on the source, and holds an altarpiece attributed to Bassano. Čara lies about 25 kilometres west of Korčula town by road, roughly 30 to 40 minutes by car, and island buses are infrequent, so it is a drive and a stop. Our pin is the register's point in the village centre rather than a fix on the trunk, and nobody has published its height or girth.

faq.q: How old is the cypress in Čara?
faq.a: Nobody has measured it. The Croatian tourist board says a century; other tourism pages say 500 years.

faq.q: How do you get to Čara from Korčula town?
faq.a: By car, about 25 kilometres west, roughly 30 to 40 minutes. Island buses run but infrequently.

orebic.intro: Above Orebić on Pelješac, about three kilometres uphill at the hamlet of Karmen, a group of cypresses surrounds the medieval church of Our Lady of Carmel, Gospa od Karmena. Croatia has protected them together as one natural monument since 1960. A walker's note calls some of them over 400 years old, a claim nobody has measured. They are not the better-known cypress stand below the Franciscan monastery, which was planted in the mid-20th century.
orebic.meta_description: The protected cypresses of Gospa od Karmena above Orebić: a group around a medieval hill church, some said to be over 400 years old.
orebic.question_meta: Orebić's old cypresses stand around the church of Gospa od Karmena on the hill at Karmen, protected as a group since 1960.
orebic.question_answer: Orebić's old cypresses are the group around the medieval church of Gospa od Karmena, Our Lady of Carmel, on the hill at Karmen about three kilometres above the town. They have been protected together as a natural monument since 1960; a claim that some are over 400 years old is unmeasured.
orebic.question_context: Two cypress stands near Orebić get confused. The protected group described here stands around the church of Gospa od Karmena at the hamlet of Karmen, on the hill above the town, and has been on Croatia's register of natural monuments since 1960 as a group of cypresses. A walker's note on komoot from 2019 calls them huge and ancient, some over 400 years old and among the oldest in Dalmatia, which is a hiker's impression rather than a measured age. The other stand, below the Franciscan monastery, is better known, and Time Out says it was planted in the middle of the 20th century. Nobody has published a count, a height or a girth for the Karmen trees. The church is reached by road or on foot by the path, about three kilometres uphill from Orebić centre, and a 2023 note says the path can be ridden on a mountain bike. We found no public transport and nothing on whether the church grounds are open. The 2023 note is the newest word on the trees.

faq.q: Where are the old cypresses of Orebić?
faq.a: Around the church of Gospa od Karmena on the hill at Karmen, about three kilometres uphill from Orebić centre, reached by road or path.

faq.q: Are the Karmen cypresses the same as the stand below the Franciscan monastery?
faq.a: No. The stand below the monastery is better known, and Time Out says it was planted in the mid-20th century. The protected old group is up at the church of Gospa od Karmena.
